title: Walking to the shop
hookLine: Thoreau's story of the saunterer: a Holy-Lander, at home everywhere
tomorrow: what did Julian hear when she was so sick she thought she'd die?

cards: Sneakers on, earbuds in, the step count ticking up as you power-walk to the corner store and back. Thoreau would slow you down. In his essay Walking, he passes on a story of where the word saunter comes from.

In the Middle Ages, he says, wanderers roamed the country asking for charity, claiming to be on their way à la Sainte Terre, to the Holy Land, until children would call out as they passed: there goes a Sainte-Terrer, "a Saunterer, a Holy-Lander."

teach.b: Whether the word truly comes from there, Thoreau doesn't prove; he calls it a beautiful derivation and moves on.
He passes on a second one too, which some prefer: sans terre, without land or a home, which in the good sense, he says, means having no particular home but being equally at home everywhere.
Then he says what he means by walking, and it isn't exercise. He sets it apart from the kind taken like medicine at fixed hours by the sick. A saunter is a small pilgrimage.
That's Thoreau's Transcendentalist teaching: the holy isn't far off in some other country. It's met here, on foot, by someone awake enough to notice.
The Holy Land is wherever your feet are, if you walk like a pilgrim. So walking to the shop can be just an errand, eyes on your phone, mind already home.
Or it can be a saunter: the same sidewalk, slower, the smell of rain on hot pavement, a neighbor's tree changing color, the cold air when the shop door opens.

how: Readers of Thoreau's 'Walking' take ordinary walks slowly and attentively, as small pilgrimages rather than exercise, noticing what's along the way.

games.q: what does “walking to the shop” mean?
o: a shortcut through the back streets home
walking slowly, as if each step were a pilgrimage
walking briskly to hit a daily step goal

p: not what Thoreau meant by walking

s: Thoreau links saunter to wanderers headed for the Holy Land
in 'Walking' he tells of a Sainte-Terrer: a Saunterer, a Holy-Lander.
Thoreau's walking was mainly about exercise
he sets it apart from exercise taken like medicine at fixed hours.
a spiritual walk needs wild country to count
the popular image. Thoreau's other story, sans terre, is someone at home everywhere.

games.q: your friend tracks every walk for pace and steps, and says slow walking is wasted time. what's Thoreau's reply?
o: a saunter isn't exercise; it's a small pilgrimage, at home wherever your feet are.
agree: Thoreau walked fast to hit his goal before getting back to writing.
walk only in the forest; for Thoreau, town streets can never count.
games.why: Thoreau tells of saunterers as Holy-Landers and sets his walking apart from exercise. the pilgrimage is the walk itself.

practice: Stand, and take a few very slow steps, across the room or in place. Feel each step land: heel, then the sole, then the toes, in time with your breath.
Let your eyes rest on one thing along the way as if you'd traveled a long road to see it.

wordCard.voice: Walking to the shop: an errand turned into a saunter. In Thoreau's story, the walker is a Holy-Lander, at home everywhere.

orig.note: French: to the Holy Land. Thoreau's story for where saunter comes from.

carryVoice: Your line: saunter, a Holy-Lander on the way to the corner shop. Day six of fourteen, sauntered.
